title: The Fair at Sarovar Ghat

setup.context: Have you ever been in a crowd so large you forgot yourself for a while? Let me tell you about the river fair at Sarovar Ghat.

paragraphs.text: Every winter the river fair fills the ghats at Sarovar. For a week there are more people on the steps than there are houses in our town. Sadhus, shopkeepers, grandmothers with flasks of tea, children who have run off from their parents.
I went as a young man to find something I could not name. I walked the steps at dawn and saw an old woman dip the same brass pot into the water nine times, slowly, as if she were counting her breath.
No one told her how to do it. Everyone around her was doing the same, in their own way. For an hour I was not a businessman or a son or a failure. I was one of many people standing in cold water.
I have never been able to describe what that felt like to anyone who was not there. I don't try anymore. I just say, go once, in winter, and stand still.

reflection.insight: Some practices work only in company. Solitude is not the only path. Being one face among thousands can loosen a knot in you that no private effort reaches.
reflection.question: When did you last feel like a small part of something bigger, in a good way?

follow_up_options: Is it dangerous in those crowds?
What happened to the old woman?

responses_to_follow_ups.danger: It can be. You keep track of your family, your shoes and your wallet, and you watch the steps. The organisers are careful. Sense matters more than courage in a crowd.
responses_to_follow_ups.woman: I never learned her name. I saw her the next year, in the same place, dipping the same pot nine times. Some people become part of a place.
responses_to_follow_ups.back: To stand still for an hour and remember I am one of many. Then I walk home and I am better at listening.
